title: Cheapest Sign Changes to Cross a Grid
statement:
Every cell of an m × n grid holds a sign telling you where to step next:

  • 1: right, 2: left, 3: down, 4: up.

You start in the top-left cell and follow the signs. A sign may point off the grid. You may repaint any sign to point another way for a cost of 1 per cell (each cell needs repainting at most once).

Return the smallest total cost that gives a path of signs from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell. The sign in the bottom-right cell itself does not matter.

examples.why: Right, right, down already reaches the corner for free.
You must go down twice and every sign points right, so two cells need repainting, for example (0, 2) and (1, 2).
The free path winds right, down, all the way left, down, and right again. Shortest in steps is not the same as cheapest.

hints: Model each cell as a node with four outgoing moves. What does each move cost?
The move the sign already points to costs 0; the other three cost 1. You want the cheapest path from the top-left node to the bottom-right node.
With only 0 and 1 weights, use a deque: push 0-cost neighbors to the front and 1-cost neighbors to the back. It behaves like Dijkstra without a heap.

explain.intuition:
Repainting a cell is the same as "moving in a direction the sign does not point to, for a price of 1". So build a graph where each cell has four edges: the one its sign points along costs 0, the other three cost 1. The answer is the cheapest path from corner to corner.

Dijkstra works, but with only weights 0 and 1 a deque is enough. A 0-cost neighbor has the same distance as the current cell, so it goes to the front and is handled next; a 1-cost neighbor goes to the back. The deque then always pops cells in order of distance, just like Dijkstra's heap, in O(m·n) time. The "each cell at most once" rule never matters: a cheapest path never visits a cell twice.
steps: Set dist to infinity everywhere except dist[0][0] = 0, and put (0, 0) in a deque.
Pop a cell from the front. If it was already finalized, skip it; otherwise mark it.

For each of the four directions d (1 to 4), let the cost be 0 if d equals the cell's sign, else 1. If the neighbor is inside the grid and dist + cost improves it, update it and push to the front (cost 0) or back (cost 1).
pitfalls: Plain BFS by step count. It finds the shortest path, not the cheapest; example 3 needs a long but free path.
Pushing 0-cost neighbors to the back of the deque. Then cells are no longer popped in distance order and answers can be too high.
Mapping the sign codes to the wrong directions: 1 is right (column + 1), 2 is left, 3 is down (row + 1), 4 is up.

solutions.title: Relax every edge until nothing changes
solutions.idea: Bellman-Ford style: sweep all cells and all four moves, lowering distances, and repeat until a sweep changes nothing.

solutions.title: Dijkstra with a heap
solutions.idea: Cells are nodes, the pointed move costs 0 and the others cost 1. Standard Dijkstra from the top-left cell.

solutions.title: 0-1 BFS with a deque
solutions.idea: Weights are only 0 and 1, so a deque keeps cells in distance order: free moves go to the front, paid moves to the back.

followups: Repainting to some directions is pricier than others (a cost per direction). Which algorithm do you need then?
Some cells are walls you can never enter. What changes in the search?
